Of this great five-syllabled mantra of the illustrious Cidambara, Sadāśiva is the seer (ṛṣi), [and] ... is the meter (chandas). (l2.)

Cidambareśvara is the *bīja* "oṃ"; "nam" is the *śakti*; "mam" is the *kīlaka*. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the recitation (*japa*) for the sake of attaining the grace of Śatambareśvara. *Hrāṃ* to the two thumbs; *naṃ oṃ hrāṃ naṃ* to the two index fingers; *oṃ hrāṃ* [to the middle fingers]; *oṃ hraiṃ śivam* to the two ring fingers; *hauṃ* to the two little fingers; [and so on] to the hands. Thus is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the heart and other limbs. *Oṃ hrīṃ hrāṃ hraiṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *hrīṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; *hrūṃ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *vauṣaṭ*.
HRAIṂ KAVACĀYA HRUṂ HRAIṂ NETRATRAYĀYA VAUṢAṬ | HRAUṂ ASTRĀYA PHAṬ | BHŪRBHUVAḤSVAROṂ—thus is the binding of the directions (digbandha).
Meditation (dhyāna):
With six arms, smeared with ashes, standing upon the dissolution of the earth, with feet held upwards...
I worship Naṭheśa, who is served by the dancing serpent-king and others, whose waist is encircled by a garland of double-tongued flames,
who is smeared with ashes, who possesses an unyielding [left] arm,
who is accompanied by Umā, who holds fire, a staff, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and who carries a hand-drum.

In the five-fold worship (*pañcapūjā*), I offer fragrance to the Earth; I offer incense to the Fire; I show the lamp to the Wind; I present the nectar-offering (*amṛtanaivedya*) to the Nectar-Self; I offer betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*) to the Reality-Self (*tattvātman*); I offer the worship of all services (*sarvopacārapūjā*) to the All-Self (*sarvātman*). The root mantra: *aṃ uṃ hara oṃ śivāya cidambaradevāya namaḥ*.

[Bālāyantra] First, one should draw a dot, a triangle, and a hexagon within a circle. Outside of that, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus and much else.
The wise know this Bālā-cakra as being endowed with four gates.
One should likewise write the three seed-syllables and the *bindu* within the triangles.
Then, one should again write them in the six corners in both direct (*anuloma*) and reverse (*viloma*) order.
Outside of that, one should write the pairs of vowels in the eight petals.
Then, by way of circumambulation in due order through that place called Bahumatrakālika,
[one should worship] Vaṭuka, the Yoginī-field, Bālā, and Gaṇapati in succession.
Having recited [the name] ending in the dative case, one should join it at the four gates:
Brahmā, meditative, stout, yellow, four-armed, and four-faced.
Having meditated thus: "The one with a swan-vehicle, four arms, [holding] a staff, a rosary, and a water-pot"—[this is] the meditation on Sarasvatī:
the goddess seated upon a lotus throne, draped in white garments.
(…) wearing a crown and holding a rosary and a book.
One should meditate upon the radiant Sarasvatī, complete in all her limbs;
having worshipped her with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should perform the yoga within the form. One should meditate on the sky of consciousness (*cidambara*).
[He is] three-eyed, possessing the cool-rayed moon, bearing the Gaṅgā, and holding a trident in his right hand and a drum (*ḍamaru*) in his left.
With his feet drawn up, possessing the splendor of a lion, and like a garment [... fearful with a mass of rays;
[he is] Māmaruka, dark as a rain-cloud, black as Time [...
[Side Heading: ... the Ritual Procedure of the Glorious Mahāśāstā-tantra ...].

For this glorious Great Teacher’s great mantra, the Seer is Ardhanārīśvara, the Deity is the Great Teacher, *hrāṃ* is the seed-syllable, *hrīṃ* is the power, *hrūṃ* is the pinning-nail; the application is for the purpose of attaining success through the grace of the Great Teacher during recitation. *hrāṃ śaṃ (…) śiṃ hrūṃ śuṃ*, etc., is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs. Thus ends the binding of the lamp. As for the visualization:
[He is] dark-complexioned, seated upon a lotus pedestal like a fresh [lotus], with his lotus-like hands holding a water-pot and a flower.
[He sits] upon a comfortable lotus seat with a yogic cloth, his left and right [hands] full and abundant.

Having performed the worship of the colors and displayed the five mudrās, one should recite the root mantra: *Oṃ śrīṃ namo hariharaputrāya pṛthulābhāya śatrunāśanāya gajavāhanāya mahāśāstāya*. Thus, having fully worshipped through the recitation of the root mantra, fire-offerings (*homa*), heating, and so forth, follows the ritual procedure for the yantra.

First, the glorious principle of the *bindu* [is] a triangle; at the tip of the triangle, a trident; at the tip of the trident, the seed-syllable of Śakti. It is surrounded by a circle of the principle of the hexagon. Outside that is a sixteen-petaled lotus; outside of that, a square with eight corners. At its tip is a trident; outside of that, on the circle, a sixteen-petaled lotus; outside of that, two pieces of birch bark. In the center of the crescent moon is the treasury of the *praṇava* mantra; at the tip of the trident is the seed-syllable of Śakti, OṂ. In the triangle is the seed-syllable of Vāla... (fragmentary).

Aiṃ klīṃ sauṃ. In the six corners [of the hexagon], [one should place] śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ śrīṃ hrāṃ klīṃ. In the intermediate spaces of the hexagon, [one should place] the root mantra of Mahāśāstā: Oṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to the son of Hari and Hara, for the attainment of a son, for the destruction of enemies, [and for the acquisition of] vehicles. Having thus encircled [the deity] in six steps by means of this mantra in a clockwise direction.

On that sixteen-petaled [lotus] (l2.), having written the sixteen vowels beginning with *a* (…), and outside of that, on the corners of the eight-petaled square, having written the eight-syllable mantra *oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya*, one should write *śrīṃ hrīṃ* at the tip of each spoke (l3.).

Outside of that, on the sixteen petals, having written the thirty-two syllables beginning with *ka* two by two, [one recites] the Gāyatrī of the Yantra: "We know the King of Yantras; we meditate upon the Great Yantra; may that Yantra inspire us. [Then] the Mantra-Gāyatrī: "We know the King of Mantras; we meditate upon the Great Yantra; may that Yantra inspire us. [Then] the Mantra-Gāyatrī: "We know the King of Mantras... (p12a. f10b).

Having written: "We meditate upon the Great Mantra; may that Mantra inspire us," and having written the seed-syllable of the eight Bhairavas from the east up to the northeast, [and] the [central] seed-syllable...

In the east, write *aṃ vrāṃ*; in the southeast, *āgne ruṃ mam*; in the south, *caṃ kaṃ*; in the southwest, *kroṃ vaṃ vuru*; in the west, *um vam vāyu mam kam so*; in the northwest, *bhīm cam*; in the north, *īśāne saṃ laṃ*. Having thus written these two sets of seed-syllables (*bīja*), thereafter, in the eight directions starting from the east, write *laṃ raṃ haṃ ṣaṃ vaṃ yaṃ saṃ śaṃ* for the world-protectors (*dikpāla*) beginning with Indra. At the eastern gate, write *gauṃ*; at the western gate, *guṃ*; at the northern gate, *duṃ*; [at the southern gate], *kṣam*.

Having thus written [the above], one should write the seed-syllable of the elephant-vehicle, *gaṃ*, outside the eastern gate of the *bhūpura*; the seed-syllable of the horse-vehicle, *tuṃ*; and having written the *pāśa*-seed-syllable on the right side of the circle outside the eight-pointed figure, and the *aṅkuśa*-seed-syllable, *kroṃ*, on the left side—thus is the *Mahāśāstā* yantra complete. It consists of ten limbs.

The ten-limbed *yantra* consists of the *jīva*, the *śakti*, the *dṛṣṭi*, the *śrotra*, the *suratnaka*, and where the *mantras* are the *digbhūtas*. The *jīva* is: *haṃ sa sāhaṃ saḥ*. The *śakti* is: *śrīm*. The *dṛṣṭi* is: *im ūm*. The *śrotra* is: *uṃ ūṃ vaśyam*. The *suratnaka* is: *klīṃ śarakmaṃ kṣo yantraṃ em*. The *mantra* is: *maṃ ik indrādi*. The *digbhūta* is: *la va ra ya haṃ*. These are the ten limbs.

Having cursed him, saying, "May he be cast into the Mukkanadi river," the Lord of the Gods vanished. (p15a, f13b, l1. [The rest of the text is blank. (p15b, f14a, l1, sideheading) [Pañcapūjā] Oṃ! To the Lord of the Universe, the savior from the ocean of hell, the bestower of knowledge, the ocean of the nectar of compassion, white as camphor, the wearer of matted hair, the pacifier of the suffering of poverty.

Salutation to Śiva, the beloved of Soma, the destroyer of poison, the ender of desire, the one worshipped by Kamalā, the three-eyed, who abides in a state beyond characteristics, the ageless, the bearer of the *kalās*, the ender of Time, whose bracelets are the lords of serpents, the bearer of the Gaṅgā, the crusher of the king of elephants, the five-faced, adorned by the king of hooded snakes, the bestower of heaven and liberation, the giver of prosperity, clad in golden garments, and adored by the three worlds.

To him who wears garments of skin, who is smeared with pure ashes, whose eyes are like lightning, who is adorned with earrings of serpents, whose feet are beautiful with anklets, whose banner is the bull; to the beloved of Rāma, the bestower of boons upon the Lord of the Raghus, who delights in dance, who is fond of music, who is meritorious, whose conduct is holy, who is worshipped by the gods, the bestower of liberation, the destroyer of sins, the Lord of the Gaṇas, who is fond of incense, whose vehicle is the sovereign bull, and who is clothed in the skin of an elephant.

Salutations to Śiva—the Great Lord, beloved of his devotees, the destroyer of the disease of worldly existence, the divine one clothed in celestial raiment, the ocean of virtues, composed of splendor, the sanctifier of all scriptures, the pacifier of poverty and suffering. This hymn has been composed by Śiṣṭa; it destroys all diseases, bestows everything upon men, and grants the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Even a slayer of a Brahmin, an ungrateful person, or one who violates the bed of his wife, child, or teacher [is purified].

One who recites this with effort and devotion shall attain union (*sāyujya*) with Śiva. Oṃ, obeisance to that Śiva, who is denoted by the syllable *Na*, who wears the lord of serpents as a necklace, whose eyes are the [three] eyes, whose body is smeared with ashes, who is the Lord of Tṛṇa, who is adorned with a garment of skin, who is the consciousness of all, the Lord of the three worlds, the destroyer of Tripura; obeisance to that Ka, Ra, Ya, Na, and Ma, for the sake of the recitation of Śiva, who is the sun to the lotus-face of Gaurī.

Oṃ, salutations to that Śiva, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, the leader of the worlds, the moon, the sun, and Vaiśvānara; salutations to that Śiva, whose syllable is *Śi*, [and who is worshipped by] Vasiṣṭha, Agastya, Gautama, and others... to the Lord of the Mountain, the illustrious Nīlakaṇṭha, whose banner is the bull; salutations to that Śiva, whose syllable is *Va*. Salutations to that Śiva, whose syllable is *Ya*, who is the very form of sacrifice, who wears matted locks, who is devoted to the Pināka bow, who is eternal, perpetual, pure, and stainless.
First, one should draw a dot, a triangle, a hexagon, and a circle. On the outside, one should draw an eight-petaled [lotus];
on the outside of that, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus and a square.
Equipped with four gates, the wise know this as the *Bālā-cakra*.
One should likewise write the three seed-syllables within the bindu and in the triangles;
furthermore, one should write them again in the six corners by way of both direct and reverse order.
Outside of that, one should write the vowels two by two upon the petals of the sun;
outside of that, having written the Mātṛkās in a clockwise sequence,
[one should place] Vaṭuka, Yoginī, Kṣetrapāla, Bāla, and Gaṇapati in order.

Now, for this *Śrī Bālāparameśvarīmālāmantra*, Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the *ṛṣi*; the Goddess Gāyatrī is the *chandaḥ*; Bālāparameśvarī is the deity (*devatā*); *aiṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*); *klīṃ* is the power (*śakti*); *sauḥ* is the pin (*kīlaka*). The application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of attaining success in the recitation (*japa*) of Bālāparameśvarī. One should perform the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*) with the root mantra.
[The] meditation (*dhyāna*) [is as follows]:

Stained by the garland of the rays of the dawn... [etc. ... *alaṃ* and so forth for the five-fold worship (*pañcapūjā*). *Aiṃ klīṃ sauṃ ṇeṃ* to the two thumbs (*tarjanī*); *sauṃ* to the two middle fingers (*madhyamā*); *sauṃ* to the two ring fingers (*anāmikā*), *namaḥ*; *klīṃ* to the two little fingers (*kaniṣṭhikā*), *namaḥ*; *haiṃ* to the palms and backs of the hands (*karatalakarapṛṣṭha*), *namaḥ*. *Aiṃ* to the heart (*hṛdaya*), *namaḥ*; *klīṃ* to the head (*śiras*), *svāhā*; [etc. ... *sauṃ* to the weapon (*astra*), *phaṭ*. *Bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ*—thus is the binding of the directions (*digbandha*).

One should join [the mantra] at the four gates of the Ācārya. In the *bindu*, one should write the *Kāmakalā*; in the abode of the triangle (*trikoṇa*), one should draw three arches (*toraṇa*). On the eight-pointed [figure], one should depict eight *suparṇas* (eagles); on the lotus of nine petals, the two ten-spoked [circles] beginning with the letters *ya* and *ā*. Having encircled the *manu-aśma-kle* [mantra], one should write this group of eight auspicious stars (*sutārakāṣṭaka*) upon the petals, numbered according to the directions. On the clear petals, one should place the vowels; on the triple circle (*trivṛtta*), one should write the *Mātṛkā* [alphabet].
One should diligently meditate upon Durgā, who is mounted on a horse, filled with the essence of dreams,
possessing eighteen arms, and situated in the center of the square.

In the *bindu* (dot), place *ī*. In the triangle, place *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*. In the eight-petaled [lotus], install the sixteen-syllable mantra (*ṣoḍaśākṣarī-mantra*) and write the fifty letters starting from *oṃ*. First, from *da* to *kṣa* (10); outside, from *ka* to *ḍha* (10); in the [eight-petaled lotus], from *ṇa* to *bha* (14). For the eighth [petal]: *a ka ca ṭa ta pa ya śa* (8). In the sixteen-petaled [lotus], from *a* to *āḥ*.

The vowel-syllable (*svarākṣara*) is *gā* in the meter; that is *sā*, *vi*, and *ti* in *Sarasvatī*. The syllable for the meter is above the city-gate (*bhūpura*), with long *svastimātrā*s for the city-gates. The consonant-syllable (*vīrmākṣara*) has ten limbs (*daśāṅga*); like the city for the *kṛtu* [meter], there are twenty. [Side Heading: Meditation on Dakṣiṇāmūrti] He who holds a *rudrākṣa* and fire in his hands, accompanied by the Lord of Stars (*uṭupati*), whose limbs are smeared with ashes, who is radiant upon a lotus-seat, whose vehicle is a bull, who wears a garland, and who is accompanied by the Gaṅgā.

whose ornaments are skins... (l5) ...to the great dancer, the wearer of the diadem.

To him who dwells in the divine abode through the cause of the gift of the wheel bestowed as a boon upon his sons by Umā; to him who is intent on protecting the wretched; to Nandin; to him whose form is perceived through the seal of silence; to him whose feet are honored by those devoid of worldly existence; to him who is auspicious through the gift of knowledge; to him whose form is [manifested] through wisdom; to him who holds the hand [of protection] against fear; to the bearer of the earth; salutation to Śiva, the auspicious one... may [this] merit lead to... [Śivastotra, Umāmaheśvarastotra] (p. 21b, f. 21a, sideheading)
To the one who bestows enjoyment and liberation, who possesses the form of Atirudra, the destroyer of Māra,
whose beloved is Śakti, and who is the support of the earth.
Salutation to Śiva, the giver of devotion. ||38||
Whoever, having risen in the morning, recites this meritorious *Śivāṣṭaka*,
a hymn to Umā and Maheśvara— *namaḥ śivābhyām*— to the two Navayappans.
By the two of them, whose bodies were locked together with one another.
Salutations again and again to the daughter of the Lord of Mountains and to the one whose banner is the bull; salutations again and again to Śaṅkara and Pārvatī. ||1||
Salutations to Śiva and Śivā, who are eager for the dance, and who,
when saluted, bestow the fruits of one's desires.
Salutations to those whose sandals were worshipped by Nārāyaṇa. ||2||
Salutation to Śiva and Umā, my two lords,
the parents of the world, whose bodies are victory itself.
Homage to the two who are saluted by the foremost of the Jambhāris; homage to the two auspicious ones who wear matted hair and support the earth,
who are expert in overcoming old age and death through gnosis.
Homage, homage to Śaṅkara, the destroyer of distress! (4) Homage to Śiva and Śivā, the carriers of the chariot!
Homage to the wise Vaiśvānara! (l. 2)
Salutations to the two lotus-faces of Rudra;
salutations to Śiva and Śivā, the supreme medicines.

Salutations to the two who possess five forms and five seeds, the auspicious Śiva and Śivā. (1) Salutations again and again to Śaṅkara and Pārvatī, who are the causes of the emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal of the manifold universe. (7)

Salutations again and again to those two who destroy the Kali age through the chanting of the Name, who possess auspicious forms at the time of their descent for the sake of devotees, and who reside upon Mount Kailāsa. (8)

Salutation to Śiva and Śivā, who wear the moon upon their crests, who bestow all prosperity, and who are honored by all branches of knowledge. Salutation to Śiva and Śivā, who grant great happiness and possess every excellence of auspiciousness. [The Hymn to Umā and Maheśvara] Hrāṃ Hrūṃ Mā...

Salutations again and again to Śaṅkara and Pārvatī, who are exceedingly beautiful, whose lotus-feet are intensely cherished by the multitude of gods, and who are uniquely and perfectly worshipped by the entire world. || 10 || Salutations again and again to Śiva and Śivā, who have the bull as their vehicle, who are well-worshipped by Viriñci, Viṣṇu, and Indra, and whose eyes are anointed with the saffron of their own divine splendor. Salutations again and again to Śaṅkara. || 11 ||

Salutations to Śiva and Śivā, the two with piercing eyes; salutations again and again to the one with the *bilva* fruit and the garland of *māmallika* flowers, and to the most excellent ones possessing the splendor of Śālāvatī and Kāntimatī. [Salutations] to Śaṅkara and Pārvatī for the fruits of fortune... [arising from] the hundred-fold... [iti]. I praise Śambhu, the Lord of Umā, the preceptor of the gods...

I praise the Lord of creatures (*paśupati*), I praise Sūrya... [the moon-crested one]... *I praise Śambhu, the Lord of Umā, the preceptor of the gods... I praise the Lord of creatures, I praise Sūrya...* [the moon-crested one]...
I salute Śrī, the Giver of Boons, and Śiva, the Benefactor. ||1||
I bow to the incomparable abode of the entire world; I bow to the one who has [acted]...
I bow to the one like the moon, beloved of the god Śiva; I bow to the favorite of Hari.
I bow to the supreme ornament of the serpent and the snake; I bow to Śiva, whose nature is consciousness; I bow to the one with the [raised] hand... || 2 ||
I bow to the one whose lower lip is like the earth, whose eyes are like lotus petals;
I bow to the one who cleaves the temples of elephants; I bow to the one whose bow is made of rock and whose string is a serpent; I bow to the one who has a quiver upon his hip.
I bow to the one who has the lotus-born as his charioteer; I bow to the destroyer of the cities; I bow to the Great One; I bow to the one who brings about the welfare of his devotees. 3.
I bow to Soma, the inconceivable, non-dual, and unborn; I bow to the pride of Kandarpa; I bow to the stainless primordial root-mantra; I bow to the dark Kṛṣṇa;
I bow eternally for the sake of the auspiciousness of Bhava.
I pay homage to the one whose form is dignified; I pay homage to the one who bestows fortune. 4.
I bow to the one born from the five faces; I bow to the moment upon his forehead; I bow to the sky-throated one with the crown of matted locks;
I bow to the bearer of the moon and the Gaṅgā; I bow to the blue-throated one... I bow to him.
I bow to that Bhāskara, who consists of six forms. ||5||
I bow to the one whose supreme abode is the peak of Mount Tāraka;
I bow to the Lord of the excellent Rādhā; I bow to the immeasurable Śaṅkara. (L4) I bow to the one who wears the earrings of the king of serpents, the destroyer of the demon Lambada.
I bow to the thousand-faced one; I bow to the one who bears the moon. (6) I bow to the incomparable one shining like Naravipra; I bow to the one consisting of solar splendor;
I bow to the thunderbolt that shatters the pride of Viṣṇu born from the lotus.
I salute Parabrahma; I salute the excellent Lord of Śoṇagiri; I salute Him who consists of all forms; I salute Bhairava. (7)
I bow to the subtle, infinite, garlanded, and fire-like one; I bow to the one whose form is the syllable *ai*;
I bow to the one praised by the bees of Rāvaṇa’s arrows.
(8) I bow to the one with the luster of gold; I bow to the one whose body is half-formed by the Daughter of the Mountain.
I bow to Śiva, the three-eyed; I bow to Bhava.
I bow to the destroyer of Kāla; I bow to Mṛḍa, the one with the matted hair;
I bow to the one who grants all goals, the ocean of the nectar of compassion.
I bow to the destroyer of the sin of drinking liquor; I bow to him whose feet are worshipped by Brahmins, gods, and demons; I bow to the remover of the loss of fortune; I bow to him [who is]... ||9||
I bow to Him who has transcended the senses, the remover of the poison of worldly existence; I bow to the one with eyes like a serpent;
I bow to this Lord of the hosts of beings;
I bow to the friend of the King of Mountains; I bow to Him whose gait is like that of a beautiful lord of fragrance.
I bow here to the one who destroyed Śūla; I bow to Karam.
(10) I bow to him who obtained his sovereignty through a sidelong glance; I bow to the beloved of Viriñci; I bow to him whose lotus-feet are worshipped by Indra and the immortals. (11)
I bow to the one whose banner bears the lord of bulls; I bow to the one adorned with necklaces and jewel-ornaments;
I bow to the beloved of Murāri; I bow to Bha...
I bow to the purifier, the stainless delighter of the Asuras; I bow to Mahādeva.
I bow to the refuge of the best of devotees, the one of excellent form; I bow to the most desired of all. (L7.
I bow incessantly to the Lord of the Destroyer of Obstacles, whose self-nature is free from [defilement], the Lord of the chest-red [one] (the Sun), the Lord of the devotees. 12.

Peaceful, [removing] the burden of birth, old age, and impurity; always bestowing the goals of Dharma, Artha, and Kāma; O God, bestowing fruits, making one pure, removing the suffering of poverty, destroying *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, and *carakas*; destroying evil, increasing longevity—whosoever constantly recites this praise shall obtain liberation from illness. Oṃ! Salutation to the auspicious, the perfect one, whose nature is adorned with cool radiance... to the Protector, who acts as the protector for all, to Brahmā, homage!

Whatever indeed... at the end of life, it is called the path to Śiva. [Thus ends the *Umā-Maheśvara-Stotra*, composed by the venerable Śrīmat Caṅkarācārya, the teacher of the wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*) of the Harasa lineage. May there be auspiciousness! At first, due to the engagement with karma, he indeed causes suffering while remaining in the state of drawing [the soul] upward; then, having ignited [it], he torments it intensely—that is, the copper-colored fire (*tāmra-jātavedas*).
Whatever suffering there may be therein, or whatever harsh object of sense is encountered, it can be [endured]...
O Śiva, Śiva, Śiva! O Bhagavān, O Śrī Mahādeva Śambhu!
(1) In childhood, even while drinking the milk of the mother, which was as sweet as nectar, there was the excessive suffering of being struck by wrestlers. (25a, f24b, l1)

Or rather, [he] is easily accessible through the senses; he who has produced the qualities of the Lord, [who] ... [is] the supreme, [who] liberates from various sufferings such as diseases and calamities, [and who is] the most auspicious Śaṅkara—I do not remember [any other] wise one, O Lord! 2. (l. 3)
I am mature, established in my own nature; yet, by the five serpents that are the objects of the senses, the young woman who is the daughter of discrimination perishes.
Or rather, one attains delicious happiness and freedom from anxiety in Śiva’s [path].
Out of delusion, I have perhaps tolerated [the loss of] my heart’s prosperity.

(3) Furthermore, in old age, when the senses have lost their power, and due to the torments of gods and others, by evil diseases, by separations, and by various corpses—[my life] is like a withered flower; and my gift is deficient.
By false delusions and desires, the mind and intellect have been rendered empty through meditation within the thicket [of existence]. (25b, 25a,
l1) It is not possible to calculate the steps of recollective action.
Whether in the Vedic tradition, in worldly affairs,
in the Dharma ordained for the twice-born, in the pursuit of Brahman which is the essence of knowledge, in the practice of righteousness,
or in the hearing and application of the [scriptures], may all [beings] be patient toward one another in my presence.
Having meditated upon that which is called Śiva in the mind— the wealth of the most excellent hero—
they offered it to the twice-born by the hundreds of thousands;
yet they did not offer it into our mouth, which is like the sacrificial fire, with seed-mantras.
He was patient with the observance of the *rudrajāpya* vow, consisting of the recitation of the *gāṅga* mantra. ||6||

(…) by those who had burnt [the body] along the middle path with hundreds of jars containing clarified butter, his limb was not established there; nor was it anointed with sandalwood and other [unguents];
nor was he honored with flowers fashioned by [artists], nor with incense, camphor, and lamps.
He should be fed various kinds of flavorful foods and drinks;
having bathed at the time of dawn, one should offer for the sake of worship the water of the Gaṅgā, which has been prepared according to the ritual rules for bathing.
In the exceedingly dense [forest], the garlands of *gandhabilvī* and *vadālī* flowers have been brought;

may they endure as a singular offering of fragrant blossoms that have blossomed with nectar. ||8|| When the limbs of the Goddess have vanished, purified and devoid of the three qualities... ||9|| (Fragmentary)

O Destroyer of Delusion, with your gaze fixed upon the tip of your nose, you who have conquered the fear of existence; I do not remember you—whose limbs are adorned by the form of self-realization—as one who possesses even a trace of the stains of wicked impurities. (9)
Having conquered the ocean [of breath] within the lotus of the heart through the practice of breath-retention (*kumbhaka*) involving the wind,
when the subtle path has dissolved into the tranquil inner self and the Great Light-form has been manifested,
that which is beyond perception is the sign (*liṅga*) denoted as the True Brahman.
It is never possible to fully behold or even endure [the sight of] the entire [deity].

(10) But those men who, endowed with excellent devotion, daily sing this hymn of praise—or listen to it—being filled with devotion to the glorious feet of Śaṅkara, shall then attain firm devotion and dispassion toward the supreme Śiva. (11)

From his own self, he manifests a bond; [he holds] in his hand a trident as bright as ten million rays of the sun, resting upon a piece of *śamī* wood within his own abode, along with a noose and an axe, and ashes; [he is] striking down the enemy from his forehead, having crushed that foe—who is scorched by the flames of fire—under the tip of his foot, resplendent with laughter... the supreme vessel of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), pure as declared in the Vedas, stainless, purified, appropriate, born of the sacred fire, immaculate, destroying sin, causing the destruction of those who seek [evil], and casting away spirits and planetary influences.
The ash, which is the body-unguent of Śambhu and the [protective] wing of the Daughter of the Mountain, bestows splendor and heroism, grants all fruits, and leads to the supreme good. 1.
Divine, fierce, manifold, unborn, eternal, adorned with Vedic ornaments, consisting of five syllables,
to be accomplished, and generating the power of one's desired goal.
He bestows the Dharma, wealth, and liberation. ||2||
The Āgneya [Purāṇa], most beloved of the Supreme Lord, to be meditated upon by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others,
and by yogins free from desire and the like; it is pure, bestows the fruit of bathing, and is praised by the Vedas— [among] those whose forms are the world.
May it provide protection for you from all sides. ||3||
For one seeking internal purification, it removes manifest diseases even externally;

it destroys the fierce great poison of impurity and the fever of passion; it is a crossing over the ocean of faults; it is an ornament for the body that generates dispassion; it is beautiful and dear to Rudra.
They are those. ||4||
A portion of Rudra, white as pure milk and the *kunda* flower, praised by the Upanishads,
the great savior from the ocean of saṃsāra, the remover of fever,
risen from the midst of the three sacrificial fires, adorned with the crescent moon, and the pacifier of negligence.
May it bring you joy at the sight of the plowshare. || 5 ||
This *Jāla* [of the Goddess] eclipses the mass of a thousand suns; it conquers all untimely death;
it subdues the messengers of Yama, the Lord of Death, and his fetters; it is a forest fire for the thickets of sin;
it is a submarine fire for the ocean of *saṃsāra*; and it is the bridge to the City of Śiva.
They belong to those men. || 6 ||
The mantra is ash, and the ash-mantra is the entirety; the ash itself is the mantra, and it is rebirth.
Ash is *bhūḥ*, ash is *bhuvaḥ*, and ash is said to be *svaḥ*;
O consumer of ashes, ash is Agni, ash is Vāyu, ash is Nirṛti, and ash indeed is the Sun and the Moon. Therefore—
May the ash, consecrated by the mantra "namas śivāya," protect the world.
(7) The three forms [of the deity] are ash, as are the multitude of qualities; the three gods are indeed ash.
Since there is no distinction between Śambhu and ash, or ash and Śambhu, within the Vedas, [ash is sacred]. (8)
Gaurī is the ash of Sarasvatī, and she is Kamalā; all the Mothers are ash.
Therefore, may the ash protect us well even from every negligence.
Night is said to be the perfection of ash, day is ash, and both fortnights are said to be ash.
Ash is the ash; he who has uttered the six seasons is that ash.
The rainy season is ash, the pair of ages is ash, even the entire kalpa is ash, and all time is ash; may that which is beyond even that—the Lord’s ash-like splendor—protect the world. 9.

The gods have always worn the ashes, as proclaimed by the words of the Vedas; everything in the three worlds is established within the ashes. When the fierce oblation is offered into Bhava, all calamities come to an end for one who is consecrated [with them].
By means of the ashes at night, malevolent spirits and planetary influences are surely destroyed; of this there is no doubt.
And by that which was released from the hand of Śiva-Śrī;

(10) [he heard] the majesty of Śiva’s ash, the meritorious heart, eternally purifying the world. Having praised and consecrated the ash with devotion while remaining in meditative absorption, [he beheld] Vārāhī mounted upon a horse, fulfilled by her dreams; Durgā and the others, Gaṇapati, Bhaṇḍana, the Vaṭukas, Vīrabhadra, the guardians of the quarters, and the one born of the [divine] host.

Laṃ raṃ haṃ ṣaṃ vaṃ yaṃ saṃ śaṃ. (L3. [The syllable for] Ugrālaśāna. (In the Vāstuśānti rite: Having performed the rites beginning with the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍasaṃskāra) up to the naming ceremony (agnināmakaraṇānta), having bid farewell to Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara, and having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should say: "Obeisance to Brahmā in the lotus of the heart" (agniṃ hṛtpadme brahmaṇe namaḥ). Having worshipped him along with his limbs (sāṅgaṃ saṃpūjya), one should offer one hundred oblations with the mantra: "To the Lord of the Vāstu and others, svāhā" (vāstvādivadhipataye svāhā). (L4–L5. Having performed the rites beginning with the consecration of the sacrificial pit up to the naming ceremony, having bid farewell to Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara, and having offered the final oblation, one should say: "Obeisance to Brahmā in the lotus of the heart. Having worshipped him along with his limbs, one should offer one hundred oblations with the mantra: "To the Lord of the Vāstu and others, svāhā."

One should offer fruits, portions of wood, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, and parched grain—one thousand or one hundred of each—concluding with the *vyāhṛtis*. [The Udvāhana of the Pitṛs: "Arise, O Fathers! Follow the ancient path of the deceased, the way of Yama. Grant us wealth and that which is auspicious; speak for us, O God, and grant us our portion. Homage to the deities of the sons! I establish you each in your proper place."

Salutation to Bhava, whose form is the earth; salutation to Paśupati, whose form is the wind; salutation to Śarva, whose form is water; salutation to Rudra, whose form is space; salutation to Īśāna, whose form is fire; salutation to Ugra, whose form is the sun; salutation to Bhīma, whose form is the moon. [The Gaṅgādharāṣṭaka] Seeing the gods, beginning with Brahmā, being consumed by the poison named Hālāhala arising from the churning of the ocean of milk, he who, out of compassion—

Fearlessly, by his own play, fashioning the worlds, he who is devoted to the protection of those in distress has protected them; that Blessed One, the Bearer of the Gaṅgā, is my refuge. (1) Striking Death upon his chest, [he established him] in his own station, solely intent on meditation.
Out of compassion, he protected the sage Mārkaṇḍeya. Having emerged from his *liṅga*, when Hari was drawn toward him for the purpose of offering the water from his eyes, he gave him the discus. 2.

Having drunk the sweet [milk] and gone to their own homes from the houses on the shore, due to the lack of milk, they perform severe penance in their minds for the sake of [obtaining] it. Out of compassion, [the Lord], intent on granting the drink of the boundless ocean of milk to Upamanyu who was distressed by thirst, [bestowed it upon him].
(…) the Blessed One, the bearer of the Gaṅgā, is my refuge. ||3||

Seeing that vast army of chariot-warriors drawn up in battle array by Droṇa and Jayadratha, the Destroyer of Suffering—who had obtained Kṛṣṇa as his companion—was overcome with great fear. He protected Pārtha, the Victorious One, while invoking his divine weapons, providing refuge for those in distress. (3–4)

Seeing a young man born of the Śiva lineage mocking his own [Śaiva] faction, and seeing him distressing his own family while raising his hands to place a mass of flowers upon his head— [the Lord], with his head bowed in the city of Viriñca (Brahmā).
He partook of the offerings of worship and food, providing protection to the distressed. ||5||
In former times, when Indra and the other gods were terrified by the fear of the *purasura* [the demon of the city], he mounted the chariot of the earth, made the Vedas his horses,
and out of compassion took up Murāri as his arrow.
Having abandoned trembling and the lack of vision, [he attains] protection from distress. ||6||
O Lord of the Universe, protect me— who am averse to following the path of the Śruti and Smṛti, who am overwhelmed by the weight of sin, and who speaks but once, "You alone are my refuge"—
for you, the ocean of compassion, were born in ancient times as the protector of those who have fallen into calamity.
Protector of those in distress. ||7||
Having seen that the Gaṅgā, which cannot be controlled by others, was being implored with great effort by Bhagīratha, who was devoted [to him],
he out of compassion [released it] upon the surface of the earth into his extended mass of matted locks.
Flooded the river, purifying the afflicted one... (8)

[Thus ends the Gaṅgādharāṣ� jewel-like Ārta-liṅga, seated within the lotus of the heart in Māyāpurī; I worship it with the ablutions of the pure water of the mind from the river of faith, with the flowers of constant meditative absorption, and with the snow-like waters of the moonstone upon its throne fashioned of a single jewel.]

O Lord, O God, O Ocean of Compassion, accept this bath, divine garments, various jewel ornaments, sandalwood enhanced with the fragrance of musk, along with jasmine, *jāti*, and *campaka* flowers; likewise, accept this offering (*bali*), incense, and lamp. O Master, accept the parasol, the two fly-whisks, the fragrant mirror, the *maddala* drum, the *kṣeri*, conch, *mṛdaṅga* drum, and *kāhala* trumpet; as well as song, dance, and water mixed with various vegetables.
O Lord, for a long time I have prepared five kinds of rice, betel, and meat as an offering for you, who are free from the two [extremes]. ||3||

For the sake of the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain, [the devotee] chooses his own body as the retinue, his home as the place of worship at the conclusion of the rite, his sensory objects as the ritual materials,
and sleep as the state of meditative absorption; the movement of the two lords [of the body and the mind] constitutes the rite of circumambulation.

O Aṅgiras, all hymns of praise—whatever action I perform, O Śambhu, let all of that be for your worship. [The Five Seats, the Lion Throne] Homage to Ādhāraśakti. In the four directions beginning with the east: Anantāsana; homage to Ananta; homage to Vāsuki; oṃ, homage to Takṣaka; homage to Kārkoṭaka. In the four directions beginning with the southeast: homage to Śaṅkhapāla.

*Namaḥ* to the pill (*gulikā*). *Namaḥ* to the lotus (*padma*). Thus is the seat of Ananta. Above that is the lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*). *Oṃ hāṃ*, *namaḥ* to Dharma; *namaḥ* to Jñāna; *namaḥ* to Vairāgya; *namaḥ* to Aiśvarya. From the east to the north, *namaḥ* to Adharma; *namaḥ* to Ajñāna; *namaḥ* to Avairāgya; *namaḥ* to Anaiśvarya. In the middle of the south and north, *oṃ*, *namaḥ* to Rājasa; *oṃ*, *namaḥ* to Tāmasa; *oṃ*, *namaḥ* to Sāttvika.

In the center: *namaḥ siṃhāsanāya*—thus is the lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*). Above that is the yoga-throne (*yogāsana*). Again, starting from the southeast and so forth: *namaḥ kṛtayugāya*, *namaḥ tretāyugāya*. [The yoga-throne, the lotus-throne (*padmāsana*), and the stainless-throne (*vimalāsana*)]. *Namaḥ dvāparayugāya*, *namaḥ kaliyugāya*. In the east, south, north, and center: *namo 'vyaktāya*, *namo niyatiniṣkalāya*, *namaḥ kālāya*, *namaḥ kalāya*, *namaḥ keśavāya*.

To the lower covering between Nairṛti and Īśāna, *namaḥ*. To the upper covering, *namaḥ*. In the center, to the Yoga-seat (*yogāsana*), *namaḥ*. Above, the lotus-seat (*padmāsana*). From the east to the north, to the stalk (*skanda*), *namaḥ*. To the seed (*bīja*), *namaḥ*. To the sprout (*aṅkura*), *namaḥ*. To the stem (*nāla*), *namaḥ*. To the thorns (*kaṇṭaka*), *namaḥ*. To the petals (*dala*), *namaḥ*. To the filaments (*kesara*), *namaḥ*. To the pericarp (*karṇika*), *namaḥ*. To the great lotus (*mahāpadma*), *namaḥ*.

Above is the stainless seat (–). On the eight petals starting from the east: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vāmā. Homage to Jyeṣṭhā. Homage to Raudrī. Homage to Kālī. Homage to Kalavikaraṇī. Homage to Balavikaraṇī. Homage to Balapramathinī. Homage to Sarvabhūtadamanī. Homage to Manonmanī. Homage to the pericarp. [In the south and north... Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of the self (ātmatattva).

Homage to Brahmā, the sovereign of the *ātmatattva* (the principle of the self). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the *vidyātattva* (the principle of knowledge). Homage to Viṣṇu, the [presiding deity] of *vidyā*. Homage to the *śivatattva* (the principle of Śiva). Homage to Rudra, the sovereign of the *śivatattva*. Having displayed the *namaskāramudrā*, one should then [offer] homage to the solar disc (*sūryamaṇḍala*) at the tip of the filaments. Homage to Brahmā, who is within the solar disc. Homage to the lunar disc (*somamaṇḍala*) at the tip of the filaments. Homage to Viṣṇu, who is within the lunar disc.

On the tip of the pericarp: *namaḥ* to the fire-maṇḍala (*vahnimaṇḍalāya*). On the fire-maṇḍala: *namaḥ* to Rudra (*rudrāya*). In the middle of the tip of the pericarp: *namaḥ* to Sadāśiva together with Śakti (*śaktyā saha sadāśivāya*). Thus is the Vimalāsana. Having meditated upon that which consists of Śiva above the Vimalāsana, [one offers]: *oṃ hāṃ*, *namaḥ* to the Heart-lotus, which is Śiva, consisting of consciousness (*cinmaya*), the seat of Śiva (*śivāsanāya*). *Oṃ hāṃ*, *namaḥ* to the Form of Śiva (*śivamūrtaye*).
